How Baccarat's Banker Commission Actually Works — and What Commission-Free Variants Change

Published October 23, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Baccarat's three main bets look deceptively plain on a felt layout: Player, Banker, Tie. New players usually clock that Banker wins slightly more often than Player and assume that's simply the better bet, full stop. It is the better bet on raw win rate — but almost every baccarat table in the world takes a cut specifically on Banker wins to cancel that advantage back out, and the exact mechanics of that cut vary more than most players realize. Understanding why the commission exists, and how different tables collect it, actually changes which version of the game is worth sitting down at.

  2. How the standard 5% commission actually gets collected

Why Banker needs a tax in the first place

Baccarat's drawing rules — the fixed script that decides whether either hand takes a third card — give the Banker hand a small but real structural edge over Player. Excluding ties, Banker wins somewhere in the neighborhood of 50.7% of resolved hands against Player's roughly 49.3%. That's not a rounding error; paid out at even money with no adjustment, Banker would be a bet with the odds tilted toward the player sitting at the table, not the house, which is exactly the opposite of how every other wager at a casino is built.

The standard fix is a 5% commission charged only on winning Banker bets, which is enough to claw that structural edge back and leave the house with a small positive edge on both sides of the table — commonly cited around 1.06% on Banker and 1.24% on Player, with the Tie bet sitting far higher, in the neighborhood of 14% depending on the paytable. The commission isn't a fee for playing Banker; it only ever applies to a winning Banker hand, which is also why it surprises some new players the first time a winning bet doesn't pay in full.

The core idea: Banker's commission exists because Banker actually wins more often than Player. Without some kind of offsetting rule, "Banker pays even money" would be a losing proposition for the casino, not a winning one.

How the standard 5% commission actually gets collected

In a physical casino, especially in traditional and high-limit baccarat pits, the 5% isn't always deducted chip-by-chip the instant a hand resolves. Many tables keep a running commission box or marker tray next to the dealer, logging what each player owes as Banker bets win throughout a shoe, and settling the total — in cash or chips — when the shoe ends or when the player is ready to leave the table. That convention dates back to baccarat's high-roller, high-limit roots, where constantly breaking a large chip stack to skim 5% off every winning hand was considered disruptive to the pace of play. Mini-baccarat tables, mass-market pits, and essentially all online and live-dealer baccarat, by contrast, deduct the commission automatically and immediately: a winning $100 Banker bet simply gets credited $95 the moment the hand settles, with no running tab to track.

Either way, the math is identical. What differs is bookkeeping, not odds — a player settling a commission tab at the end of a shoe isn't getting a better or worse deal than one paying it hand by hand, just a different payment rhythm. The one practical risk of the tray system is human: it's on the player to confirm the tally before cashing out, since a running tab that spans dozens of hands is easier to lose track of than an automatic per-hand deduction.

A worked example with real numbers

Say you bet $100 on Banker and the hand wins. At a standard commission table, you're paid $95 — the full $100 stake back, plus $95 in winnings, for 5% of the win withheld. Bet that same $100 on Player and win, and you're paid the full $100 in winnings with nothing withheld, because the commission only ever applies to Banker. Over a long enough session, the lower combined odds of winning on Player roughly offset the extra 5% you keep on every Player win, which is exactly why the two bets land so close together in house edge despite paying so differently on a single hand.

BetWin probability (excl. ties)Payout on a winApproximate house edge
Banker (standard commission)~50.7%0.95 to 1 (5% withheld)~1.06%
Player~49.3%1 to 1~1.24%
Tie~9.5%8 to 1 (varies by table)~14.4%

Commission-free variant one: pushing on a Banker 7

The best-known commission-free structure, often sold under the EZ Baccarat name, removes the 5% withholding entirely and pays every winning Banker bet at full even money — with one carve-out. If Banker wins specifically with a three-card total of 7, the bet pushes instead of paying out at all. That single carved-out result does almost exactly the same job the 5% commission was doing: it claws back just enough of Banker's edge, concentrated into one specific, relatively infrequent outcome, to land the game's house edge close to where a standard commission table sits.

This structure is usually paired with a side bet — commonly called Dragon 7 — that pays long odds specifically when Banker wins with that three-card 7, turning the one outcome that costs the main Banker bettor a push into a separate, optional, high-variance wager for anyone who wants to bet on it directly.

Commission-free variant two: the half-pay Banker 6

A second, increasingly common commission-free structure takes a different outcome and handles it differently instead. Here, every winning Banker bet pays full even money except when Banker wins with a total of 6, which pays at half odds — 1 to 2 — rather than even money. Functionally, this is the same idea as the push-on-7 rule: pick one specific winning outcome that occurs often enough to matter and reduce it rather than touch every single Banker win. Because a winning Banker 6 happens more often than a winning Banker 7, reducing its payout to half rather than pushing it entirely is enough to do the same edge-correcting work with a smaller single-outcome penalty.

This version tends to show up heavily in Asian-market casinos and has become common in online baccarat specifically because it requires no commission tray, no running tab, and no end-of-shoe settlement — every hand pays out in full immediately, with the one reduced-payout exception built directly into the paytable rather than tracked separately.

StructureHow it claws back Banker's edgeNeeds commission tracking?
Standard commission5% withheld on every Banker winYes (tray or per-hand)
EZ-style, push on Banker 7One specific winning result pushes instead of payingNo
Half-pay Banker 6One specific winning result pays 1:2 instead of 1:1No

So which version should you actually play?

None of the three structures is a meaningfully better bet than the others in the long run — that's the entire point of the adjustment, in each version. Casinos calibrate the push rule, the half-pay rule, and the straightforward 5% commission to land in roughly the same narrow house-edge range on Banker, give or take a small amount depending on the exact paytable in use. What actually changes between them is session experience, not expected value: a commission-free table never requires tracking a running tab or interrupting play to settle up, a push-on-7 table adds a natural, built-in side-bet hook for players who want extra action, and a half-pay-six table can feel like a "bad beat" the first time a seemingly winning hand pays half of what a player expected, even though nothing about the underlying math has changed.

The one thing worth double-checking at any unfamiliar table, physical or online, is which structure you're actually playing before you sit down — a Banker bet's real-world payout on a 6 or a 7 depends entirely on which rule set is posted, and mixing up a commission table with a commission-free one mid-session is the easiest way to misjudge what a winning hand is actually worth.

Frequently asked questions

Is a commission-free baccarat table actually better for the player than a standard table?

Not meaningfully. Casinos design commission-free structures — whether a push on a Banker 7 or a half-pay Banker 6 — specifically to land in roughly the same house-edge range as a standard 5% commission table. The difference is mostly in how the math is delivered, not how favorable it is.

Why do some commission-free games only pay half on a Banker win with 6?

Because a winning Banker 6 happens often enough that reducing its payout to 1-to-2 instead of even money claws back roughly the same edge that a flat 5% commission on every Banker win would otherwise take, without requiring any commission tracking.

What is the "Dragon 7" bet and how does it relate to EZ Baccarat?

Dragon 7 is an optional side bet, commonly offered alongside EZ-style commission-free tables, that pays long odds specifically when Banker wins with a three-card total of 7 — the exact outcome that pushes rather than pays on the main Banker bet in that format.

Does the Tie bet change on a commission-free Banker table?

Not directly. The commission mechanics described here apply specifically to the Banker bet; the Tie bet's payout and house edge are set independently and vary by casino regardless of which Banker structure is in use.

How is baccarat commission actually collected at a physical casino table?

It depends on the pit. Many traditional and high-limit tables track what's owed on a running marker or commission box and settle it at the end of a shoe or when the player leaves. Mini-baccarat and most online tables instead deduct the 5% automatically the moment each winning Banker hand resolves.
